title: Chapter 20
paragraphs: Vronsky was staying in a roomy, clean, Finnish hut, divided in two by a partition. Petritsky was billeted with him in camp. Petritsky was still asleep when Vronsky and Yashvin came in.
"Get up — stop sleeping," said Yashvin, going behind the partition and giving Petritsky, who lay with hair tousled and his nose in the pillow, a prod on the shoulder.
Petritsky jumped abruptly to his knees and looked around.

"Your brother was here," he said to Vronsky. "He woke me up, damn him, and said he'd come back." He pulled the rug up and flung himself back on the pillow. "Oh, shut up, Yashvin!" he said, furious at Yashvin for tugging the rug off him. "Shut up!" He rolled over and opened his eyes. "You'd better tell me what to drink — the taste in my mouth is foul, it's...."
"Brandy is better than anything," Yashvin boomed. "Tereshtchenko — brandy for your master, and cucumbers!" he shouted, obviously enjoying the sound of his own voice.

"Brandy, you think? Eh?" Petritsky asked, blinking and rubbing his eyes. "And you'll have one too? All right then, we'll drink together! Vronsky, will you have a drink?" said Petritsky, getting up and wrapping the tiger-skin rug around himself. He went to the doorway in the partition wall, raised his hands and hummed in French, "There was a king in Thule." "Vronsky, will you have a drink?"
"Get going," said Vronsky, putting on the coat his valet handed him.
"Where are you off to?" asked Yashvin. "Oh, here are your three horses," he added, seeing the carriage drive up.
"To the stables — and I have to see Bryansky too, about the horses," said Vronsky.

Vronsky had in fact promised to call at Bryansky's, about eight miles from Peterhof, to bring him some money owed on some horses, and he was hoping to fit that in as well. But his comrades realized at once that he was not going only there.
Petritsky, still humming, winked and pursed his lips, as if to say: "Oh yes, we know your Bryansky."

"Mind you're not late!" was Yashvin's only comment; and to change the subject: "How's my roan? Holding up?" he asked, peering out of the window at the middle horse of the three, the one he had sold Vronsky.
"Wait!" Petritsky called after Vronsky as he was on his way out. "Your brother left a letter and a note for you. Hold on — where are they?"
Vronsky stopped.
"Well — where are they?"
"Where are they? That's the question!" Petritsky said solemnly, moving his forefinger up from his nose.
"Come on, out with it — this is silly," said Vronsky, smiling.
"I haven't lit the fire. They're around here somewhere."
"Enough fooling. Where is the letter?"

"No, I've honestly forgotten. Or was it a dream? Hold on — hold on! What's the use of getting angry? If you'd drunk four bottles yesterday the way I did, you'd forget where you were lying. Wait a moment, I'll remember!"
Petritsky went behind the partition and lay down on his bed.
"Wait! Here's how I was lying, and here's how he was standing. Yes — yes — yes.... Here it is!" — and Petritsky pulled a letter out from under the mattress where he had hidden it.

Vronsky took the letter and his brother's note. It was the letter he had been expecting — from his mother, scolding him for not having been to see her — and the note was from his brother saying he needed a short talk with him. Vronsky knew it was all about the same thing. "What business is it of theirs!" he thought, and, crumpling the letters, he stuffed them between the buttons of his coat to read carefully on the way. In the porch of the hut he was met by two officers; one from his regiment and one from another.
Vronsky's quarters were always a gathering place for all the officers.
"Where are you off to?"
"I have to go to Peterhof."
"Has the mare arrived from Tsarskoe?"
"Yes, but I haven't seen her yet."
"They say Mahotin's Gladiator's gone lame."
"Nonsense! But how on earth will you race in this mud?" said the other.
"Here come my saviors!" cried Petritsky, seeing them enter. The orderly stood in front of him with a tray of brandy and salted cucumbers. "Yashvin here is ordering me to drink a pick-me-up."
"Well, you really put us through it yesterday," said one of the new arrivals. "You didn't let us sleep a wink all night."

"Oh, didn't we wrap it up nicely!" said Petritsky. "Volkov climbed onto the roof and started telling us how sad he was. I said: 'Let's have music — the funeral march!' He fell flat asleep on the roof to the funeral march."

"Drink it up; you absolutely have to drink the brandy, and then seltzer water and plenty of lemon," said Yashvin, standing over Petritsky like a mother making a child take medicine, "and then a little champagne — just a small bottle."
"Now that makes sense. Hold on a moment, Vronsky. We'll all have a drink."
"No — goodbye, all of you. I'm not drinking today."
"Why — putting on weight? All right, then we'll have to do it without you. Give us the seltzer water and lemon."
"Vronsky!" someone shouted when he was already outside.
"Yes?"
"You'd better get a haircut — it'll weigh you down, especially on top."
Vronsky was in fact starting prematurely to thin a little on top. He laughed gaily, showing his even teeth, and, pulling his cap down over the thin spot, went out and climbed into his carriage.

"To the stables!" he said, and was just pulling out the letters to read through, when he thought better of it and decided to put off reading them so as not to distract himself before looking at the mare. "Later!"
